criteria.note: The single most useful phrase, in Korean with translation and a copy button, appears in the first ~80 words, and the allergy-framing rationale follows immediately — exactly what a searcher for 'korean gluten free phrases' wants.

Title is 53 chars with the rendered ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix, description ~135 chars, keyword present in both, and the description adds angle (reconfirmation, copy-and-show) rather than repeating the title.
Headings carry the argument — allergy beats gluten-free, reconfirm, name hidden sources, then situational blocks, then an explicit limits section — so a skim reproduces the piece's thesis.

Four contextually earned internal links (hidden gluten, label guide twice at the exact points where reading a label is the fallback, /places, celiac travel guide), each placed where the reader would actually need it.

All five FAQ answers are established in the body — the 밀가루/밀 distinction, the no-pronunciation stance, 알레르기 유발물질 on labels, and the cross-contamination limits — and each stands alone as a rich result.

Concrete but thin: one dated-ish window (2025–26), one quantified anecdote (10% wheat), and a region (Seoul and Gyeonggi), but no named venue, no specific dates, and the central 'year of asking' claim carries no countable detail.
criteria.evidence_quote: during our first year back in Korea (2025–26), one bakery owner told us — cheerfully, without being pressed — that his was 10% wheat

criteria.note: Korean terms are glossed and romanised where a reader needs them (간장 soy sauce, 고추장 gochujang, 양조간장 brewed, 혼합간장 blended), and the checkable specifics — Sempio 501, 고시 제2025-60호 — are precise enough to verify.
Both external claims are anchored to primary sources with dates: the Sempio product page (retrieved August 2026) and the MFDS labelling standard with notice number and 29 August 2025 date.
A dedicated section states what the method cannot establish ('no sample, no measurement, and no lab test'), the household's NCGS status is disclosed up front, and there are no affiliate links.

findings.quote: across a year of asking, we did not meet a single server or bakery owner who treated 글루텐프리 as a medical constraint until we changed the word
findings.why: The piece's central experiential claim — the one the whole allergy-framing argument rests on — has no countable or datable substance behind it: no approximate number of venues, no districts, no month range, no instance where the framing failed. As written it reads as a generalisation rather than an observation, which is the weakest form of first-hand signal for E-E-A-T.
findings.fix: Attach one or two verifiable anchors to that year: roughly how many restaurants/bakeries were asked, over what months, and at least one named or describable venue where 글루텐프리 got a shrug and 알러지 got a kitchen check. Similarly, date and locate the 10% wheat bakery anecdote (district and month at minimum) so it stops reading as an unplaceable story.

findings.quote: Two habits that came out of doing this badly first
findings.why: The piece gestures at having got things wrong but never shows the failure — a specific misfire (a dish eaten, a reaction, a phrase that backfired) is the highest-value experience signal available and it is being withheld here.
findings.fix: Add one sentence describing the actual bad outcome that produced these two habits — what was ordered, what the staff said, and what happened afterwards.

findings.why: This line sits inside a post whose stated method is that you should not pronounce anything, and it directly cuts across FAQ 3 ('Don't — show them instead... this guide gives no pronunciation guide at all'). A reader landing on the FAQ rich result and then the body meets two different instructions in the same document.
findings.fix: Reword to the show-don't-say frame, e.g. 'Either is fine to show — 알레르기 if you're copying from a label, 알러지 if you're copying from here.'

findings.quote: The literal translation is 글루텐프리, and it is the phrase least likely to get you a useful answer.
findings.why: FAQ answer 1 runs well past the length a Google FAQ rich result will display, so the parts that matter most to the searcher — show 밀가루 알러지, ask about 간장 separately — sit past the truncation point.
findings.fix: Front-load the actionable instruction in the first 150–200 characters of the answer and move the 밀가루-versus-밀 caveat to the tail, or split it into a separate FAQ entry.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is either sourced (Sempio, MFDS) or explicitly flagged as first-hand pattern, but the traditional soy sauce composition claim is neither.
criteria.evidence_quote: Traditional **조선간장 / 한식간장** — the meju-based kind used for soups and namul — is soybeans and salt in its classic form.

criteria.note: Product names, notice number, dates and the year-of-observation anecdotes are internally consistent and point to checkable primary pages.
States exactly how it knows (a year of asking as a couple, one GF person) and names what that cannot establish — no sample, no measurement, no lab test.
No absolute guarantee anywhere, cross-contamination handled in its own section and in the FAQ, and the household's NCGS reality is explicitly separated from coeliac requirements.
Both external sources carry retrieval dates and notice dates, and reformulation plus staff turnover are flagged as reasons an old answer expires.
Labelling law and terminology are right, but the hand-over block asks in 밀가루 terms where the article itself established 밀 is the operative word, and the English gloss hides the mismatch.
criteria.evidence_quote: 밀가루, 보리, 호밀 전부 못 먹어요.

criteria.note: Gives a concrete self-check path — read 원재료명 in hand via the label guide, and phone ahead for restaurants — rather than requiring trust in the author.

findings.quote: 밀가루, 보리, 호밀 전부 못 먹어요.
findings.why: The body establishes that 밀가루 means wheat flour specifically and that brewed soy sauce carries 밀 the grain, so a kitchen can honestly deny 밀가루 while serving wheat. The save-block — presented as the version that gives 'the whole picture at once' — reopens exactly that hole, and repeats it in the soy sauce line ('간장이나 고추장에 밀가루가 들어가는 경우가 많아서요'). The English gloss compounds it by rendering 밀가루 as 'wheat'.
findings.fix: Change the block to '밀, 보리, 호밀 전부 못 먹어요' and '간장이나 고추장에 밀이 들어가는 경우가 많아서요' (keeping the 밀가루 allergy opener if desired), and align the English gloss so 밀가루 reads 'wheat flour' and 밀 reads 'wheat'.

findings.quote: Traditional **조선간장 / 한식간장** — the meju-based kind used for soups and namul — is soybeans and salt in its classic form.
findings.why: This is a factual composition claim about a product category that is neither cited nor marked as the authors' own observation, unlike the 양조간장 claim beside it which carries a Sempio source and retrieval date. The following hedge about 혼합간장 keeps it from being decision-driving, but the asymmetry in sourcing is visible.
findings.fix: Attach a source for the traditional composition (an MFDS 간장 식품유형 definition or a manufacturer ingredient page), or mark it explicitly as the authors' shelf observation the way the assume-wheat rule is marked.
